lines: Somewhere in every big project, there's a handful of tasks that can happen whenever, and a handful of others that are stuck waiting on several things to finish first.
And buried in that mess is a single number: the fastest the whole project could possibly be done.
That number turns out to be nothing more than the longest path through a graph this chapter already knows how to build.
Here's the trick this topic runs: visit every vertex once, in the order a topological sort already hands you, and relax its edges on the way past. No queue, no repeats.
Now, what happens to that trick the moment the graph has even one cycle hiding in it somewhere?
answer: It breaks, and it breaks silently.

A topological order only exists because nothing points backward. Take that away, and a vertex can get locked into a final answer before one of its own predecessors has even been visited — and this algorithm never goes back to check.

lines: So here's the mechanism, one vertex at a time, strictly in that order.
By the time you reach any given vertex, every edge coming into it has already been relaxed by everyone upstream who could possibly make it better.
That's the whole proof, really — not a clever trick, just the order itself doing all the work.
Watch what happens if you relax those same edges, on that same graph, in some other order instead.
One vertex gets its distance locked in early — too early — and ends up stuck on a number that's simply wrong.
No crash, no warning. The algorithm finishes and hands you an answer that looks exactly as confident as the right one would have.
Flip the sign on every single edge weight, run the identical pass, and shortest paths become longest paths.
Does that same move work on any graph at all, or only on this particular shape of one?
answer: Only here — only where there's no cycle to begin with.
Flip the sign on a cycle of positive weight and you get a cycle of negative weight. A negative cycle means there's no bottom to find — loop it forever and you keep improving.
A graph with no cycle at all never has that problem, which is exactly why this one substitution is safe here and nowhere else.

lines: A project's own task graph can never have a cycle — a task can't wait on itself finishing first, directly or by some roundabout chain.
So its critical path, the one everybody in project management talks about, is nothing more exotic than the longest path through that graph.
Same algorithm, same single pass, just read off as the answer to a different question.
Every other algorithm in this chapter had to earn its answer the hard way — a priority queue, round after round of relaxing, an entire reweighting step just to get rid of negative edges.
This one needed none of that, because the one thing it demanded up front — no cycles, anywhere — ruled out every problem the others were built to survive.
The cheapest algorithm in the whole chapter, and it's the one that asked for the most to begin with.
